title: Optimize the chip for SMP throughput rather than a single very large core
decision: Use two processor cores on one chip, sharing a large unified L2 cache, rather than concentrating the transistor budget in one monolithic processor.
rationale: The design was explicitly optimized for high-throughput SMP workloads. The authors argue that server workloads commonly provide enough independent processes to keep multiple processors busy, while additional transistor investment in extracting instruction-level parallelism has diminishing returns. Sharing the L2 on-chip also provides much greater latency/bandwidth for data sharing than discrete processors could achieve.
outcome: POWER4 integrates two independent out-of-order processor cores and a shared L2 on one die, providing chip-level thread parallelism while retaining substantial single-thread instruction-level parallelism.
quote_as_recalled: SMP optimization: The server must be designed for high-throughput multitasking environments.
weakest_point: The paper states the SMP-oriented objective and resulting two-core/shared-L2 organization, but the strongest explicit 'two smaller CPUs versus one big one' formulation comes from contemporary POWER4 material rather than this journal paper.

title: Make very high clock frequency a first-class design objective
decision: Revamp the chip design and system organization specifically to support best-of-breed operating frequencies, while designing the surrounding system so that balance can be preserved as processor frequency increases.
rationale: The authors regarded leadership processor frequency as an explicit objective rather than treating frequency as merely an implementation consequence. They used new transistor-level design tools, transformed complex control logic into more regular dataflow structures, and designed the system so future technology improvements could raise processor frequency without destroying system balance.
outcome: POWER4 was delivered at 1.1 and 1.3 GHz, with the system buses intentionally operating at lower fractions of processor frequency to maintain the required system balance.
quote_as_recalled: We planned from the outset to deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies.
weakest_point: This captures the stated frequency philosophy, but I cannot confidently reconstruct a more detailed journal-paper passage describing a specific frequency-versus-pipeline-depth alternative.

title: Treat RAS as a system-design principle rather than simply adding ECC and reliable components
where_in_paper: Guiding principles / reliability, availability, and serviceability
decision: Design RAS pervasively across hardware, firmware, and operating-system behavior, with the objective of avoiding outages and converting situations that would traditionally cause a checkstop into recoverable software-visible errors where possible.
rationale: The authors explicitly rejected the narrower philosophy that high reliability could be obtained merely from reliable parts and ECC in major arrays. They wanted redundancy and recovery mechanisms that could circumvent failures, and emphasized continuous server operation.
outcome: POWER4 incorporated pervasive fault detection, recovery, isolation, redundancy and deferred repair, including mechanisms that transformed certain hard machine stops into synchronous machine interrupts to software.
quote_as_recalled: we accepted the principle that one does not achieve high levels of reliability only by choosing reliable parts
weakest_point: The exact wording of the quoted fragment is reconstructed from the paper text available in search results; the detailed RAS mechanisms are also discussed more fully in the companion paper cited by Tendler et al.

title: Use a distributed-switch interconnect instead of a conventional centralized switching structure
decision: Build the SMP interconnect as a distributed switch implemented through point-to-point bus structures, allowing POWER4 chips to be combined into systems up to 32-way without a separate centralized switching component.
rationale: The system was designed as an architecture spanning multiple chips rather than as an isolated processor. The interconnect had to provide the bandwidth and low latency needed for shared-memory SMP while fitting the physical/package constraints of the POWER4 design. Distributing the switching function across the chips avoided requiring a separate external switch structure.
outcome: POWER4 systems could be constructed from four-chip multichip modules and interconnected modules, with the distributed-switch topology supporting systems up to 32 physical processors.
quote_as_recalled: The interconnect topology, referred to as a Distributed Switch, is new to the industry.
weakest_point: The paper clearly identifies and describes the Distributed Switch, but my characterization of a conventional centralized switch as the rejected alternative is interpretive; the paper does not explicitly present that alternative as a rejected design.

title: Protect L1 data with parity while relying on L2 for recovery
where_in_paper: Cache hierarchy / reliability and error recovery
decision: Use parity rather than full ECC for the L1 data cache, while guaranteeing that L1 data is also present in L2 and using the store-through policy so a corrupted L1 line can be discarded and refetched from L2.
rationale: The hierarchy was structured so that L1 errors could be recovered without losing data: inclusivity guarantees an L2 copy, and store-through ensures updates reach L2. This permits parity protection at L1 while L2/L3 use ECC, with firmware recovering an affected L1 line by flushing and refetching it.
outcome: POWER4 implemented parity-protected L1 data cache with inclusive, store-through L2 behavior, while L2 and L3 used Hamming ECC for single-error correction and double-error detection.
quote_as_recalled: The L1 data cache is parity protected, through inclusivity and a store-through design.
weakest_point: The source text clearly states the mechanism and recovery path, but it does not explicitly frame parity-versus-ECC as a formal rejected alternative in the decision-making narrative.
